[h1][u]TLDR:[/u][/h1]
Persona 5 Royal (P5R) is one of the best modern JRPG's to play, though it does have its flaws. The game features a unique story, fun characters, strategic turn-based combat, an amazing original soundtrack, and romance, all wrapped in an impressively stylish presentation. It takes an average of 80+ hours to see pretty much everything so be prepared for a significant time commitment. The game can be incredibly easy if you decide to use the free DLC content. Kasumi's content feels tacked on rather than integrated with the original P5 story. 

Most importantly, thanks to ATLUS for finally learning that porting their popular games to PC is a good business decision.

And, RIP Billy Kametz, voice of Dr. Maruki, who died just before the game's PC launch. 

[h1]GENRE:[/h1]
Turn-based, life-sim & dungeon-crawling JRPG

[h1]GAMEPLAY:[/h1]
P5R takes place over a calendar year where on almost any given day, you are (mostly) given free reign to do anything during the given time of day (usually you get some combination of a morning, afternoon, and evening) as time progresses on. Usually, you attend school during the morning, which features simple classroom segments of answering obscure trivia, get the afternoon to do whatever, and then later on in the story you can leave your home to do things in the evening. Things you might choose to spend your time doing may include activities that raise your personal stats (e.g. knowledge, charm, etc.), interacting with your friends and confidants to level up your relationship ranks to unlock unique perks, optional training in a dungeon when that is unlocked, and more.

On the dungeon crawling side, the main story progresses when you complete palaces, which are hand-crafted (not procedurally generated like previous Persona games) dungeons full of dangerous enemies and bosses. Palaces can take a decent amount of time to complete depending on how resource friendly you decide to be when it comes to items and SP management, but they can be doable within one day (unless the story forces you out to come back later for plot reasons). In the palaces, you fight using your personas, which are basically demon allies with magical powers, in turn-based combat.
Generally, the flow of the game is to encounter a new villain, complete a new palace, wait during downtime for the next villainous encounter, and repeat.

As the protagonist, you are able to use more than one persona, unlike your party members. You can get new personas by negotiating with them in battle or by fusing two or more personas at the Velvet Room. Throughout the game, you will gain access to more powerful Velvet Room activities and fusion methods to create more powerful personas and build them the way you want.  

[h1]STORY:[/h1]
In P5R, you are a high-school transfer student (typical Persona start) moving to Tokyo, Japan. Unfortunately, you have been unfairly charged as a criminal due to a past incident, and everyone seems to treat you like you are an outcast. On your first day of school, you somehow wander into some strange castle and meet an obnoxious, unclothed man named Kamoshida who captures you and your friend and orders your executions. Backed into a corner, you suddenly hear a voice in your head, and you manifest a powerful being known as Arsene! 

Where did these powers come from? Who is Kamoshida and what is that castle? Who was the corrupt man that branded you as a criminal when you did nothing wrong? And, is any of that connected?

When Final Fantasy XV launched back in 2016 it started with a message - "A Final Fantasy for Fans and First-Timers”. And while it can be argued if that is true in regards to the FF franchise, I feel that saying works really well for Persona 5. If you never played a Persona title, you can jump straight away without any fear, and what you’ll find is a game that is incredibly addictive and it definitely deserves the title “one of the best JRPGS of all time”.

On a personal level, Persona 5 is one of my favorite games of all time, I’ve played through it numerous times and I still can’t believe that I’m doing it right now on PC. Something that was a pipe dream years ago turned into reality and I never would’ve missed the opportunity to support Atlus’s decision to finally put the game on Steam.  I still can’t quite comprehend how much the series has grown since that fateful day in late 2007 when I was introduced to Persona 3 by a close friend. It was like nothing that I’ve played before and I loved it so much, that I went back and played Persona 1, 2 and numerous SMT titles, and then eagerly anticipated the release of Persona 4. When I played Persona 4 Golden for the first time back in the day, I thought that was the pinnacle of what the Persona franchise can achieve, but Atlus has shown us they have more than enough gas in the tank to keep this train going with Persona 5.

The game feels much like a second home, while the outside world remains turbulent as ever, Joker and company are there for you if you need some entertainment to wind down. The characters feel like real people with real problems that are willing to test your empathy all through this 100-hour adventure. Persona 5 doesn’t just focus on the glam, it does the mundane really well. There are moments where you’re cleaning up your room, going out with a friend, or having your depressed guardian take you to school. You get used to just chilling and taking it all in, because every moment in this adventure counts and you foolishly start to understand it only when the end credits are starting to roll. 

The story is another strong point and while some moments seem predictable, it doesn’t take away from its glory. Dungeons are improved compared to Persona 4 and they are separated in two categories campaign related and side content (which remain procedurally generated). The gameplay/combat animations are incredible and even something incredibly mundane as getting the upper hand in a battle seems smooth and stylish (even more in 120fps!). The soundtrack is brilliant and yes, during the years this has become a tradition in almost every Persona/SMT game and thank God it is, because it helps tremendously to set the mood.

Persona 5 Royal is a collection of many things: inspiring stories, good times with good friends, a stunning visual novel and an amazing dungeon crawler. By working on what was already great and with brilliant new additions, Persona 5 Royal is an unforgettable experience that has you thinking about it long after it’s over.

[h1]So good that I bought it 4 times[/h1]

I know my reviews are long and I appreciate the time you taking the time in reading them. 

I own Persona 5 on the PS3 and PS4, Persona 5 Royal on the PS5 and on PC. Look I’m fully aware that by buying every re-release of a game I’m part of a problem in today’s gaming industry. Gamers being squeezed for every last penny they’ve got, more so with fans of a particular game or series. “They love it, so they’ll buy it anyway”. And Atlus certainly has proven itself to be part of that side of the gaming industry that wants their fans to pay the absolute maximum, because they know that we’ll buy it anyway.
It's just that most of their games are some of the absolute best ever made, and Persona 5 Royal, for me, is probably on top of that list. It’s everything I hoped a game would be as a kid and here’s why.

[h3]A childhood dream come true[/h3]

When I was a kid I used to read tons of comics, hundreds of them a year. My parents bought me a little tape-player (yes, I’m that old) and every last cent of my pocket money was spent on either comics, music, or audiobooks on tape. It was much cheaper than buying a CD and the selection they had on certain events was just insane. Laying in bed listening to every story over and over again, my eyes closed and imagining I was part of every journey. No matter if I was Tintin, Spiderman, Wolverine or Asterix, I loved every story and I’ve been a part of many of them.

I wasn’t all too familiar with Atlus-games in 2016, but I saw a trailer for Persona 5 and immediately added it to my wishlist on the PS-store. The more I checked out some early-on impressions on YouTube and read about it, I became aware of the huge passion the fans of the series had. Apparently the Persona series (and ofcourse Megami Tensei as a whole) had quite the legacy, which only made me more excited to play the game. 

In April 2017 I was sitting on my couch, watching the download of Persona 5 crawl along. I felt something that I felt when unwrapping a new comic or tape. A mix of anticipation, excitement and a hint of nervousness. It’s done. The Atlus logo is displayed, the music starts, goosebumps. And suddenly I’m not sitting on my couch anymore, I’m part of the Persona universe, each morning I’m waking up in an attic, I’m Ren/Joker.

[h3]Masterful storytelling[/h3]

Ren’s a high school student accused of assault and therefore put on probation, his parents decide that he’ll go to another school and stay with their family friend Sojiro Sakura. There he’ll become part of a story where adults are taking advantage of their (social) positions, most of the time to the detriment of children/young adults. Ren/Joker gets to know these victims, befriends them and starts to form his own social circle in this new city. Adults who become so distorted by their own (wicked) desires form a so-called palace. A place where they are the rulers and anything what they want to be in real life becomes reality, influencing their behavior in the real world. Ren and his friends infiltrate these places (palaces) and try to take away the thing that feeds these adults to behave the way they do (a treasure). 

Persona 5 does an impeccable job sucking you in their world. The way the story unfolds is on a level I’ve experienced maybe a handful of times in gaming. Yes, it’s a slow burn the first couple of hours but with good reason. The game starts in the middle of the story and after you are introduced to the stories’ setting you are thrown back to the beginning. So many questions arise: Why was I there, what was I doing in a casino of all places, who betrayed me? 

When you get to the free roam part of the game you’re several hours in. It’ll definitely be worth it, but if you’re more into the ‘dive straight into the action’-type games, be aware of this. But I hope you can find the patience because otherwise you’re missing out on one of the greatest stories ever told.

Persona, for me, feels like I’m reading a comic and all of a sudden I’m part of the story and certain choices have an impact on MY friends, on MY town, on MY family. I don’t want to disappoint any of them, which make some of the choices so hard and so genuine. Who to spent time with? Who to date? Who to deepen your bond with? To balance all these choices while also trying to improve your own (social and combat) skills feels just like real life. I don’t want to say no to any of them, but I’ve got to think of myself as well you know?  I am Ren/Joker, these choices are mine and I must deal with the consequences. 

[h3]Perfect gameplay[/h3]

P5(R) stays true to the turn based genre and to earlier Persona and to most of the Megami Tensei games. If you’re familiar with them than P5R brings very little new stuff to the table, but it’s probably also the reason you’ll love this one. The game is divided in 2 forms of gameplay. 

First the dungeon crawling, action focused gameplay takes place in palaces/Mementos. Here you’ll face ‘shadows’, fight them, gain new (fighting) skill and collect new additions to your team. Second is social part of the game, here you can explore the city, train social/life skills and socialize with a wide variety of people struggling with society. These social connections are a large part of what makes P5R so great. Each of the social connections has their own backstory. Some struggle with past mistakes, some with financial issues, are being bullied or are even unaware of who they really are. With each step you get to know them more and just like a real friendship they try to help you along in life, just like you‘re helping them. 

The balance between the 2 gameplay types is great. Whenever you reach the limitation of certain confidant/social storylines the main storyline advances. Giving you several hours of action-filled gameplay, which advances everyone’s story and gives you a new purpose to focus on when the social aspect again becomes the main focus. This ebb and flow of different kinds of gameplay keeps you invested, interested and makes it hard to stop. There’s always something new to see, learn and love just a couple of minutes away.

In the last 6 years I’ve played P5 (including Royal) 7 times. Depending on the difficulty setting and your interest to explore every part of each confidant, it should take you anywhere from 70 to 120 hours to complete. New game plus lets you keep items and social skills from the previous playthrough, which gives you more time to deepen the relations with the people around you and encourages you to choose an increased difficulty.

[h3]I’m not crying..[/h3]
The amount of times I’ve had goosebumps from profound emotional moments is insanely high. Moments where you can’t help but yell at the screen be it from happiness, anger of sadness. And when the story reaches it’s inevitable peak and conclusion it felt like I was saying goodbye to my own friends and family. You know that feeling when you’re watching the last scene of ‘Friends’ (or another series that’s close to your heart), ‘Embryonic Journey’ by Jefferson Airplane starts playing and you feel the tears welling up in your eyes. You’re torn somewhere between a feeling of love, loss and happiness to have been part of something truly special.

P5R does that to you. It makes you want to instantly play the game again but also to keep a distance for a while because it takes time to recover from something that you so deeply love but eventually has to end.

This is the greatest game I have ever played. I have never written a review for anything, let alone a game before. Before playing persona 5, my personal greatest games were the Last of Us and Fallout New Vegas, with many other greats right behind it, but putting this game above them was one of the easiest decisions I have ever made (I have Ellie's tattoo and the wild wasteland perk tattooed on my damn body mind you). I have never felt the things I did about any other game before. I, a 23 year old man, have never in my life cried for as long as I did than after the credits started to roll. I beat Royal two days ago and still when I boot up my laptop I can't find the strength or desire to do anything but boot up Persona and either stare at the title screen or cut it up in the thieves den (little trinket hub side feature).

 Other than yapping about how this game has completely consumed my every waking thought, I will yap about why this game is so perfect. Every single feature is as perfect as the definition of the word. The soundtrack, I can't even find the words to describe how amazing the soundtrack of this game is, those words might not even exist in the English language (I don't wanna say perfect too much). The soundtrack is so good than you don't even need to play the game to appreciate it, but when you do and finally have experiences to tie each song to, and each track just gets ten times better. I will 100% be listening to this soundtrack for the rest of my life. And the art, oh my god the art of this game, from the little screen of Tokyo between each day, the MENUS AAAAAHHHHH the menu art of each confidant, speaking of which, each confidant, don't even get my started. 

As sick as the story itself is, the real beauty of this game is the relationships you build with all the people you meet, and (literally) saying goodbye to them and moving on from this game is one of the most difficult things I have ever had to do. I don't even want to touch on the story itself because I think everyone should go in as blind as I did, but just trust me when I say it is absolutely incredible. It has so much that goes into it that one thing I realized is that you actually can't spoil Persona 5 with a single sentence, there is just too much that happens. But every story beat, and every twist they throw at you is just nothing short of master class, and dawg I'm telling you, I have never in my life been quite as lit as when I was fighting the last like 5 bosses. 

I have truly screwed myself over, because for the rest of my life I will compare every game, and even every piece of fiction, to Persona 5 Royal, and I'm sure every single time, those other works will never be able to come anywhere close to the experience of playing this game for the first time. This is one of those things that if i had selective amnesia, and I could choose one thing to experience for the first time ever, I'm picking Persona 5 Royal every. single. time. 

I can talk about this game forever, and I probably actually will, but as far as this review goes, no one is gonna read this, I can't foresee a situation where anyone comes to this store page without the intent to purchase the game, I'm not changing anyone's mind or anything here, and I will likely be the only human to ever read these words, but I had to take the time to write this. My final save file is about 215 hours long, and I will cherish each and every second of those 215 hours for as long as I live, and it has permanently rewired the way my brain works. If for some reason you are reading this and are on the fence, please, please play this game. And if every loading screen telling you isn't enough, please, Take Your Time.

[h1] Persona 5 Royal, the Game that stole my heart [/h1]

When I started the game on December 2024, I wasn't really familiar with how ATLUS Games work and I was really overwhelmed of how the game works, there was so much to do and as a perfectionist, I always wanted to do the right thing which made me not know how to play the game correctly. That unfortunately, made me stop playing the game for a while for multiple times and start other games, and also not to forget I started on a hard difficulty and I had a tough time against the first Palace Boss, which led me to quit the game for a while. Thankfully I had a lot of people who taught me how to play the game correctly, and that is where the fun started. I would like to thank @Ardelle @liliphobic and especially @Zaferius since he taught me most of the stuff! I have finished the game a couple days ago and I already started a NG+ for the love of Story and the characters, to get 100% achievements and also playing on a harder difficulty for a challenging experience, literally a 11/10 experience, especially since I haven't been spoiled on the Story (rare case to be honest).

[h2] The Story [/h2]

it's about High schoolers that have difficulties in life because of Adults, either because of their impact or what they personally did to them, so the High schoolers Rebell against that and fight, for a better future and a better world.
It's a Story about fighting the broken evil World, also finding about their true selves, heal from the past and getting to know real friends with true friendships. Royal added so many details about it than the original game, especially the 3rd Semester with the perfect Villain. His Story was so very different than the others and the fight was also different, which made it interesting, VERY INTERESTING.

[h2] The Characters [/h2]

Fabulous, Elegant, Magnificent, a Masterpiece. I played a lot of games with great casts, but there is always that one or 2 that I disliked or hated. But in the case of Persona 5, there is no such thing. I LOVED EVERYBODY HERE!
The more you get to know a character, doesn't matter if you spend time with them to strengthen your bonds with them or get further in the Story, they all get likeable at a time, to be honest I liked everyone from the start and I starting to love them after a while in the game. Spending time with them is a great option to get to know the characters better, also their stories since it gets to the direction of what they want to become in the Future.
Their stories are serious, emotional, funny, and wholesome. Literally the whole package. Also not to forget the romance, absolute cinema. Literally with every girl you try to romance it's so well made, sensational! What I really wish is that when you get into a relationship with someone, it gets Canon in the game. Like the whole group acknowledge it and not just say "we are just friends" although they are more than that. Please ATLUS make that happen in the future projects!
I also want to mention [u]Makoto Niijima[/u] is best girl <3

[h2]A Stylish Masterpiece of Strategy and Snark[/h2]
This game is the ultimate mashup of a JRPG, a high school simulator, and a heist movie—but with a talking cat and a killer soundtrack. It’s as stylish as it is stressful, because nothing screams “fun” like balancing school, friendships, and stealing the distorted desires of corrupt adults.

[h3]Story[/h3]
You’re just an average high school student—or so you thought. Wrongly accused of a crime and shipped off to Tokyo, you stumble upon the Metaverse, a magical dimension born from human desires. Here, you and your new crew, the Phantom Thieves, dive into the minds of shady adults to steal their wicked hearts. It’s like Inception, but with more jazz music and fewer Leonardo DiCaprios. Along the way, you’ll unravel conspiracies, form unbreakable bonds, and get yelled at by a talking cat for staying up too late.

[h3]Strengths[/h3]
[b]✔️ Combat That Makes You Feel Like a Genius[/b]
Every battle feels like a perfectly choreographed dance of flashy moves and tactical brilliance. And when you land a critical hit and trigger a stylish All-Out Attack, it’s impossible not to cheer for yourself.

[b]✔️ Characters You’ll Want to Be Besties With[/b]
The Phantom Thieves are basically the coolest friend group you’ve ever dreamed of joining. Whether it’s the sweet and awkward artist Yusuke or the bold and feisty Ann, you’ll find yourself rooting for them—and maybe even tearing up once or twice.

[b]✔️ A Soundtrack So Good It Should Be Illegal[/b]
With tracks like "Last Surprise" and "Rivers in the Desert," this soundtrack will live in your head rent-free for weeks. Good luck resisting the urge to hum "Take Over" during your next grocery run.

[b]✔️ Visuals That Put Other Games to Shame[/b]
From slick menus to explosive combat animations, everything in this game is so stylish it could walk the runway. Seriously, even the pause menu is cooler than most other games.

[b]✔️ The Stress Simulator You’ll Love to Hate[/b]
Planning your days, managing your social life, and deciding whether to hang out with your friends or infiltrate a palace will give you flashbacks to finals week—but in the best way.

[h3]Weaknesses[/h3]
[b]❌ The Calendar Will Haunt You[/b]
Did you waste an entire day playing darts with Ryuji instead of studying? Too bad, because now you’ll be up at night regretting your poor life choices.

[b]❌ Morgana’s Bedtime Rules[/b]
Want to stay out late and train for the next boss fight? Too bad. Morgana will scold you until you go to bed. Sleepytime police strikes again.

[b]❌ Time Will Disappear[/b]
You’ll tell yourself, “Just one more in-game day,” and then suddenly it’s 3 a.m. and you’re questioning all your life decisions.

[h3]Achievements[/h3]
The achievements are like your to-do list: intimidating but oddly satisfying to check off. From maxing out your relationships to mastering combat, every task feels rewarding. And don’t worry—nothing is missable if you plan well. Just… maybe don’t waste time playing darts with Ryuji.

[h3]Target Audience[/h3]
[b]✔️ Recommended for[/b]
• JRPG fans who love strong characters and flashy battles
• Players who enjoy balancing a full schedule while stealing hearts
• People who want a game dripping with style and humor

[b]❌ Not Recommended for[/b]
• Gamers who hate time management (or calendars in general)
• People who dislike talking cats (seriously, why?)
• Those who don’t want to spend 100+ hours on a single game

[h3]Final Verdict[/h3]
This game is a dazzling mix of strategy, storytelling, and pure style that will keep you hooked from start to finish. Whether you’re drawn in by the heists, the friendships, or the endless jazz bangers, you’re in for a ride you won’t forget. Oh, and let’s not forget: it’s the best Persona game to date. The bar has been raised—and it’s now in the Metaverse. 🎭✨

[h1][b]Stealing Hearts, Rewriting Fate: Exploring the Magic of Persona 5…[/b][/h1]
» [b]Persona 5 Royal[/b] is a massive, gorgeous JRPG with well over a hundred hours of gameplay for completionists. With more to do than ever and the series’ most compelling narrative yet, it stands out as an extraordinary, memorable experience and easily one of the deepest JRPGs of the last decade. Its sprawling dungeon design and stylish, fully realized world are an absolute joy to explore, and even after two playthroughs and the Platinum trophy, I find myself itching to go back to try different dialogue options or revisit particularly fun puzzles. This is a new gold standard for Japanese RPGs and by far the best entry in the series.

[h1]Story[/h1]
» In stark contrast to the slow burn of epic-length cutscenes that greet you in previous games, Persona 5 starts its long journey with a bang by throwing you directly into a fast-paced foot chase through a vibrant, stylized Tokyo casino. As we are introduced to the complex yet approachable turn-based battle system in those opening moments, series fans will recognize not only returning systems from Persona 3 and 4 but also long-absent elements like ranged weapons and negotiation that haven’t been in a Persona game in over a decade, adding more depth and variety to combat. Persona 5 is the culmination of everything the JRPG series has been building to, with familiar elements dialed up to 11 and some welcome new surprises added into the mix.

In what is by far the series’ strongest story to date, Persona 5 puts you in the capable shoes of a high school student who spends his evenings saving the world. By day, you will attend class, answer quiz questions, and live the life of a typical teenager, but after school you will see the clever concept of invading the minds of corrupt adults who are up to no good and battling psychological demons in order to change their hearts.

[h1]Environment[/h1]
» The game’s stand-out dungeons take place in “palaces” created within the mind of each target, and [i]ATLUS[/i] takes advantage of this to set them in diverse and outlandish places. Unlike the procedurally generated halls of Persona 3’s Tartarus or Persona 4’s Midnight Channel, Persona 5’s labyrinths are fully hand-built and feature unique puzzles and mechanics that vary with the theme of each dungeon and never repeat. A museum, for example, has very different security measures than a medieval castle, and you will find very different enemies in a pyramid than you might in a spaceship. This gives each palace a sense of identity tied to the target and provides some smart, unpredictable story moments and challenges.

[h1]Gameplay and Characters[/h1]
» Persona 5’s sense of scope is staggering compared to the dungeons in Persona 3 or 4, with palaces easily double or triple the size of those previous areas. While Persona 4 has you run through linear hallways until you reach the top of a dungeon, Persona 5 has branching paths, networks of hidden rooms, doors that require puzzles to open, and even excursions to other parts of the cognitive world outside of the dungeon itself. Starting each new dungeon is a bit daunting, but solving puzzles and progressing to each new area offers a wonderful sense of accomplishment.

While the chemistry between the characters never quite reaches the heights of Persona 4’s Scooby Gang vibe, Persona 5’s more cohesive main story does allow each character to shine in individual moments instead, exploring troubled pasts like the loss of a parent to add weight to present day scenarios. This series has never shied away from exploring serious subject matter, and here it sheds light on abuse by teachers, drug sales, suicide, and a host of other issues that are handled well and are at times extraordinarily moving. Each character’s motivation for joining you is relatable and unique, and even each palace’s target has believable conviction. 

[h1]Combat[/h1]
» Battle in Persona 5 is a familiar turn-based formula, with melee attacks, ranged weapons, and magic attacks based on one of eight elements. A bit like catching Pokemon, you collect Personas that you will use to fight, and each has its own unique set of skills as well as its own set of strengths and weaknesses. While each of your party members has one permanent Persona to use, the protagonist has the lone ability to hold multiple Personas at once. This means that you can acquire additional Personas to use as you progress, and collecting multiple Personas with different abilities is a fun way to tailor your play style to the type of combat you prefer. You can also fuse combinations of Personas to create new ones, which allows you to inherit certain skills until you have created the Persona that is right for you.

[h1]Social Life[/h1]
» While Persona 5 is a solid modern turn-based JRPG first and foremost, it also quickly becomes an interesting time-management simulator. When you are not saving the world, your time after school is your own. You are able to visit hub districts within Tokyo for activities like training at the gym, fishing, working a part-time job, batting practice, seeing a movie, or just heading home to study, play a retro game, or reading one of dozens of books. These activities are a gigantic improvement upon the comparatively limited amount of things to do in Persona 4 and a fun way to expand your personal stats like Charm, Guts, or Kindness.

On top of social activities, you also have 20 Confidants to spend time with, forging bonds with fellow students or other citizens of Tokyo. As you level up these bonds you will earn relevant stat increases and gameplay advantages that are surprisingly robust. Spending time with a speech-giving politician, for example, might help your negotiation skills while training with an arcade’s light-gun expert helps your expertise in ranged weapons, and a local board game champion will give you new strategies in battle. Balancing Persona 5’s many activities with maintaining these social links (which can only be advanced on specific days) is a welcome challenge and will require methodical notetaking for anyone who wants to maximize each day of the calendar.

[h1]Art and Design[/h1]
» The very act of exploring Persona 5’s Tokyo is a delight. From city lights at night to crowded subways during your school commute, every part of this world is bursting with vibrant color, and every detail feels meticulously thought out and eerily accurate to real-world Tokyo. The anime-like art style is complemented by full animated cutscenes that are absolutely gorgeous and help to punctuate major story events.

Each area of Tokyo feels completely distinct, with the major hubs of Shibuya, Shinjuku, and Akihabara each offering aesthetic differences on top of locations reminiscent of their actual real-life counterparts. Shinjuku features a seedy dive bar in contrast to Shibuya’s family-friendly diner, and Akihabara is home to an arcade and shops for buying games and electronics. As the subway-themed map begins to fill in, you get a sense of just how much there is to do in Tokyo compared to Persona 3 and 4’s relatively tiny Tatsumi Port Island and Inaba.

All of this is further enhanced by Persona 5’s impressive sense of style. I found myself flicking back and forth in menus over and over simply to appreciate the slick transitions. Sharp design choices permeate even tiny details of gameplay, like scenic changes that vary based upon your mode of transportation as you leave each area, or a free-flowing results screen after victory in battle.

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
» Ultimately, Persona 5 is an exceptional JRPG and an absolute must-play that has spectacular storytelling, gameplay, and design. With its incredible sense of scope, style, and detail, this is perhaps one of the greatest JRPGs ever made and stands as the best entry in the series.

[h1]Introduction[/h1]
Persona 5: Royal, or P5R ongoing, is a JRPG/anime fusion that focuses primarily on storytelling and character building, all the while trying to strike at some rather bleak and overall graphic material, such as drugs, sexual violence and even murder. Will you listen to your Persona and become a Phantom Thief of hearts?

[table]
[tr]
    [th][b]🟩 Positives[/b][/th]
    [th][b]🟥 Negatives[/b][/th]
[/tr]
[tr]
    [td]🟩 A beautifully written and flowing story that succeeds at delivering emotional impactfulness without ever letting your pulse drop. There are so many elusive secrets to it that will take diligent observation to unveil.

🟩 P5R is an enormous game with so many things to do. I will run short of words covering it all, but should you give this title a chance, be sure to try as much as you can.

🟩 Approximately 3/4 of the game takes place in the 3D animated world Atlus has designed. The last 1/4 or so is presented through anime scenes that give you a momentary reprieve from controlling the situation and allow you to take it in.

🟩 One of the best soundtracks to any video game I've ever played. Truly spectacular and adrenaline-inducing the entire way through.[/td]

    [td]🟥 Long cutscenes and time advancements make it hard to save in-between heavy plot points. It doesn't happen often, but when it does, the weight of it all can get to you.

🟥 The game is on a time limit. You have to complete everything you want to within a certain timeframe. It can be a turn-off for some people who don't like to be paced or micromanaged like that.[/td]
[/tr]
[/table]

[h1]Story[/h1]
You experience the story of P5R as a self-named hero (canonically Ren Amamiya or Akira Kurusu, if that sort of stuff bothers you) who was wrongly convicted and sentenced for a crime he didn't commit. On his probation, he is sent away to live with a guardian in another city, and it's there, the story truly begins to unravel.
Shortly after arriving in his new temporary hometown, he begins to slip in and out of an alternate dimension, known as the Metaverse. It is there that he awakens to the awesome power he held within his heart, his very own Persona, Arsene, breaks forth from his chains, and thus the first of the Phantom Thieves is born. With this newfound mask and his ever-growing group of followers, he seeks out injustice in the world and steals the hearts of villains to change their wicked ways and repent.

Truly, this is such a remarkable story. It has been masterfully written and designed to provide you with an unforgettable experience no matter your choices. I wanted to touch on so much above, but I think it's best if it's only a brief overview of the game rather than anything too in-depth. This is one of those stories better experienced than being told about.

[h1]Gameplay Analysis[/h1]
[b]Don the mask of the Phantom Thieves.[/b]
There is a literal plethora of activities and subtle secrets to uncover around the world, from playing at the batting cages to working a part-time job for the much-needed cash in the early stages of the game. You will never be bored or short of activities as PS5 attempts to keep you busy pretty much the entire way through without letting you catch your breath.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2966894471

P5R focuses on making you earn your place in its world through decisions, where every bond you build will cost you something else as time ticks towards the endgame. I'd recommend playing the game as you want to for the first playthrough, then maybe using a guide for the NG run to try and experience everything you can if you're so invested.

[b]Power that lurks in the dark.[/b]
P5R will have you spend a decent portion of your game time, lurking in the darkened halls below the city, in a Metaverse reality called Mementos. This is essentially a free-roam area where you can keep descending till you eventually reach the bottom in the very late game. You can gather materials, experience points and gold here, so it's perfect for farming for those requirements when needed. It's also important to note that some of the most formidable enemies you will face in the game appear down there, so go prepared before you descend too deep.

[b]Let us go where the fight takes us.[/b]
On the back of talking about difficult foes, we might as well talk about combat and how that ebbs and flows throughout the game. You will end up with a relatively large retinue of followers by the end of P5R, but you can only really ever use 4 of them at a time for standard combat scenarios. Each party member has their proficiencies and weaknesses and should be used with that in mind, by taking a fiendishly weak to electricity character into an electrical boss fight will only end badly. It can also work extensively in your favour if you can deduce the enemy's weaknesses and strike at them often to down enemies and unleash all-out attacks for tremendous damage or complete baton passes to increase your damage and take advantage of the additional turns.

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2966894338

On top of the weaknesses and strengths, you will also have an array of different skills to use in combat, such as gun abilities (which will never be your bread and butter but are pretty cool still), Persona abilities, melee attacks, guarding and analysis for all your different needs, and the main combat UI is pretty clean giving you only critical information to monitor about the fight itself.

[b]You are only as strong as the bonds you tend.[/b]
It is crucial to your success in this title to increase your bonds and friendship as much as you can, in the time you have, especially of those in your group. They will improve their abilities and become far more versatile and imposing entities if you put the time in to cultivate them. People outside of your group will provide you with extraordinary capabilities that will improve your chances of victory

[quote]Wear your mask proudly and head to, [url=https://store.steampowered.com/curator/43064204/] Hell, Purgatory and Paradise[/url] to experience your very own awakening.[/quote]
I started this game to change the hearts of others, but in the end, it was my own heart that was changed...

[H2]Introduction:[/H2]

I first played Persona 5 many years ago on PS4, enjoyed it very much and came close to finishing it, but unfortunately I had a lot of things going on at the time, so I had to put it aside. Alas, the console broke down before I could return to it, and I had moved away from PlayStation hardware in favor of PC gaming. Fortunately, the improved Persona 5 Royal version eventually went multiplatform, thus enabling me to play the very best version on the most powerful hardware available.

[H2]Visual Presentation:[/H2]

Being originally developed for the PlayStation 3 hardware, Persona 5 was never a game which featured cutting-edge visuals, but nevertheless the game's stylized artistic direction manages to make Persona 5 a visually interesting game. Persona 5 features colorful graphics set in the distinctive style of Japanese Anime with a combination of fully animated 3D models as well as 2D animated portraits for each of the major characters, complete with both in-game rendered 3D and 2D anime cutscenes. As a result, P5R looks like a combination of a Visual Novel and a 3D Japanese Role-playing Game, which is likewise reflected in the gameplay, but we'll get more into that later.

[H2]Audio Presentation:[/H2]

Persona 5 Royal features multiple musical tracks, consisting of both orchestral melodies as well as complete songs, each with English language lyrics. The music sounds good and the songs are extremely catchy, provided that you can appreciate Jazzy tunes, lounge music, and Japanese Pop. The in-game dialog is available in your choice of either Japanese or English, with all critical, plot-significant dialog and story sequences featuring full voice acting. The English Dub is best described as adequate, the performances aren't outstanding, but they suit the characters well and the lines are well spoken. I haven't sampled the Japanese Dub, but I'm unqualified to comment on it regardless because I don't speak the language.

[H2]Gameplay Mechanics and Features:[/H2]

Persona 5 Royal is a combination of a traditional Turn-based JRPG, Dungeon Crawler, and a Life Sim/Visual Novel in which you must balance a daily schedule of attending High School, spending time speaking with friends to strengthen your bonds with them, exploring dungeons and engaging in traditional turn based combat with enemies. As you would expect from the aforementioned combination of genres, the game is extremely dialog heavy, including sequences in which you must answer questions in class, engage in conversation with friends, and carefully choose your responses from a multiple choice dialog tree in order to answer questions correctly as well as get closer to your friends. You also have a variety of stats directly associated with social interaction — Knowledge, Guts, Proficiency, Kindness, Charm — which directly effect your ability to express yourself. These stats are increased by engaging in various daily activities as well as interacting with particular individuals, and are fortunately in most cases gained passively from average everyday activities, so you don't have to invest too much time into increasing them. Interacting with your friends increases the Rank of your bond with them granting various perks in combat and allows you to fuse more powerful Personas to equip yourself with.

The JRPG portion of the game is likewise exactly what you would expect from the genre. You explore dungeons, (Palaces) engage in turn-based combat with enemies (Shadows) with a variety of techniques at your disposal, earn Experience Points to Level Up along with money to buy equipment, and open treasure chests to gain loot in the form of various items. The only variation to the standard JRPG formula lies in the eponymous Personas, Mythological Entities which are equipped to you and your party similarly to weapons, granting magical abilities. Personas level up passively along with you when equipped, but have their own separate stats. Those who have played various Monster Taming RPGs will be familiar with the basics here, but it isn't difficult for newcomers to learn through progression.

Altogether, the combination of genres compliment each other and makes for an engaging, multifaceted gameplay experience which can seem deceptively overwhelming at first but quickly becomes second nature in practice.

[H2]Story:[/H2]

In Persona 5 Royal you take on the role of a teenage boy who has been moved away from his home out in the country to live with a family friend in the city after he became involved in a confrontation with a drunken man who was attempting to force a young woman into his car, with the man injuring himself in the process and the boy arrested then charged with assault. The boy arrives in the city only to find that his undeserved reputation as a juvenile delinquent has followed him there, with his new guardian addressing him as an unwelcome guest, his teachers at school likewise dismissing him as a delinquent, and his classmates avoiding him while exchanging rumors regarding the details of his arrest.

Shortly after his arrival, he discovers a mysterious App has appeared on his Phone which seems to restore itself no matter how many times he deletes it. One day on his way to school the App is inadvertently activated during a conversation with another ostracized student, transporting them into another world in which the School has been replaced by a Palace ruled by the School's abusive P.E. Instructor, with the two being locked up in the dungeon by the guards. They escape their cells with the help of a mysterious feline creature named Morgana, but are quickly caught by the guards on their way out of the palace, leading to the boy awakening to his Persona — his "other self" — granting him the power to defeat the palace guards and escape. The next day they return to the Palace where they are informed by Morgana that it exists within the mind of its ruler as a cognitive manifestation of his distorted desires, and that by stealing his treasure they can change his heart, thus putting an end to his abusive behavior. From there the trio forms a team known as The Phantom Thieves of Hearts, setting out to use their powers to reform society by changing the hearts of various corrupt authority figures, recruiting new allies along the way as they are drawn ever deeper into an insidious plot to seize control of Japan by manipulating the masses.

[H2]Performance:[/H2]

Being a port of a game which was originally developed for the PlayStation 3, Persona 5 Royal doesn't require a particularly powerful PC to run. I encountered no performance issues whatsoever over the course of my 171 hour long playthrough and the game ran flawlessly at Max Settings on my PC. Your experience may vary based on the specs of your PC, but I can safely say that there are no bugs, glitches, or performance issues to speak of regardless.

[H2]Final Verdict:[/H2]

Persona 5 Royal is an excellent game featuring many hours of content between the deep, engrossing story and entertaining assortment of gameplay mechanics. I came just short of a 100% run, missing only a single Confidant, yet completing the story and side quests in their entirety, closing out the game by earning 100% of the Achievements. My playthrough lasted 171 hours, thus making it by far the longest of any single player game I have ever played in 35 years of gaming. I enjoyed the game thoroughly and am left with nothing bad to say about it whatsoever. I highly recommend it to anyone seeking an immersive JRPG to occupy their time.

[h1]It seems this is the limit of humanity[/h1]
After years of wanting to play [b]Persona 5 Royal (P5R)[/b], [b]Atlus[/b] finally made the game available for PC and it’s by far the longest turn-based [b]JRPG[/b] I have played. There is so much content for me to cover, and I don’t think this review will do this game justice on how much there is available.

[h1]Pros and Cons[/h1]
[b]Pros[/b]
[list]
[*]A fantastic story that will teach you the meaning of freedom
[*]Great characters that have impressive development and personality
[*]Fun turn-based combat with many unique abilities
[*]Lots of stuff to do in the overworld
[*]Awesome soundtrack that is just nice to listen to
[*]Beautiful graphics and unique style to the visuals
[/list]

[b]Cons[/b]
[list]
[*]The dialog is a bit weird during the cutscenes
[*]Getting the best ending in the game is a bit cumbersome
[/list]

[h1]Story[/h1]
The story starts out with [b]Ren Amamiya[/b] (you can change his name) who was falsely accused of assault one night when trying to defend a woman. He is then labeled a criminal and is now on probation as well as sent to [b]Sujin Academy[/b] where he will continue his second year of High School. He moves into the attic at [b]Cafe Leblanc[/b] thanks to the help of [b]Sojiro Sakura[/b] who is taking care of him for his probation period. He also gets his first new friend at his new high school who goes by the name of [b]Ryuji Sakamoto[/b].

That is all I will go into for the story of P5R, there is a lot for me to talk about and it would take at least half of this review to even talk about the beginning portion of the game. The story is just outright fantastic, and the characters shined greatly. They made the story just outright fun, with my three favorites being Ryuji Sakamoto, Yusuke Kitagawa, and Goro Akechi. I liked their personalities and how they all go along. There are other characters I liked as well but those three shined to me the most. I could make an entire review on the characters alone for the game, as there is just so much to talk about with them and the story.

The only issue I had with the story is how some of the dialog is presented in the game. This mainly stems from the English dub. There are times when characters will say "this means in English" while speaking English; I know they are in Japan but it just sounds awkward. I don’t mind if the dialog is changed in English dubs a tad bit and this is coming from someone who does prefer their subs over dubs. I was just too used to playing the Persona games in English when I started with P4G. This is, of course, my opinion only and you can play the game in whatever language you prefer.

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
The gameplay for [b]P5R[/b] is probably one of the hardest things for me to explain in this review as there is so much to talk about. However, I will go over combat first as that is the main gameplay feature of the game. In combat, you and your party members will have a certain [b]Persona[/b] with their own abilities, as well as a weakness to another ability. This also applies to the enemies that you will encounter as well. If you, a party member, enemy, or boss exploit a weakness, they will get an extra turn to do whatever they want. 

However, new to [b]P5[/b] (as this feature was in the original version) is the [b]Baton Pass[/b] feature, which allows a party member who exploited a weakness to allow a different party member to attack. This can be useful in some battles if different enemies have different weaknesses, so if one enemy is weak to ice and the other to wind and you have two party members or if [b]Joker[/b] (who is [b]Ren Amamiya[/b]} has a [b]Persona[/b] who can cover those weaknesses and already had his turn. The [b]Baton Pass[/b] mechanic is a handy feature that I recommend you take advantage of. You can also get some extra benefits from [b]Baton Passing[/b] as well, like restoring some HP, SP, and doing extra damage. However, you do need to hang out with your party members to get these benefits.

During combat, [b]Joker’s Personas[/b] will stop learning moves, what you can do then is go to Igor, who will then fuse your unwanted [b]Personas[/b] into new and more powerful ones. You can get new [b]Personas[/b] after battle but the method of getting them is different. [b]Shuffle Time[/b] has been removed and now you need to try and talk your way to understand the enemy and if both of your responses go along with what the enemy is feeling, you get a new [b]Persona[/b].

If you knock all the enemies down in combat, then you can do these [b]All-Out Attacks[/b]. These attacks will damage all enemies while doing physical damage, this will bypass physical immunity or resistance if the enemy has it. 

However, there is lots of stuff for you to do outside of combat, you can spend time together with your party members or other friends. This will increase your [b]social links[/b], which can be used for helping give the [b]Personas[/b] you fuse extra levels and experience, which will make them stronger than usual and they may learn a few extra useful moves as well. Your party members will also learn new abilities in combat that will help you out in certain situations, so I highly recommend you go out and hang out with everyone as much as you can.

You will also get requests to help other people out in [b]Mementos[/b], this is another area of the game that you can use to farm your [b]Personas[/b] and party members. I also recommend doing these as you can get some nice rewards when exploring the place which can be very useful in combat. Your party members will also have some conversations sometimes with each other that add to their character altogether.

Although, I do have one issue with the game and that is the method of getting the true ending of the game, which is entirely unique to [b]P5R[/b]. To get this ending, you need to max out three social links in the game and to add to this [b]Goro Akechi’s[/b] social does not progress in the story like in the original [b]P5[/b], you must hang out with him. All of these have a time limit, but the game gives you more than enough time to get all three of them maxed out, so there is that. It’s still cumbersome to do though, as you can’t really miss a day to hang out with at least two of them. One of the [b]social links[/b] you can max out with no issue as it’s small and that character is also unique to [b]P5R[/b] but the other two you must hang out with when they call you. This is not a big issue but something that still annoyed me, nonetheless.

[h1]Soundtrack[/h1]
The soundtrack for [b]P5R[/b] is honestly one of the best things of the game, every song I listened to was just fantastic and I loved them all. My favorites have to be [b]Life Will Change, Rivers In The Desert, Take Over, Last Surprise[/b], and [b]Ark[/b]. As you can tell, that is a long list of my favorite songs in the game, they are all honesty great.

[h1]Graphics and Performance[/h1]
[b]P5R[/b] is a beautiful game both in its 2D and 3D art style, I loved looking at all of the games areas it has to offer. I tested the game on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1060 3GB, AMD Ryzen 5 1500X Quad-Core Processor 3.50 and 16 GB of RAM. I experienced no issues while playing which ran at a smooth 60 FPS.
https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=3051310040
[h1]Final Verdict[/h1]
If you are looking for a great turn-based [b]JRPG[/b] with a lot of depth and obvious care from the developer, then I highly recommend [b]P5R[/b]. There is a lot to do in the title and this review does not do the game justice, at best, I have only talked about at least 10% of the game itself and it’s only because I can only fit so much into a review without risk of spoiling the story. If you want to uncover what this game has to offer, the only thing I recommend is to play the game yourself.

GAMEPLAY: 4.5/5
The gameplay of Persona 5 Royal encompasses... quite a lot, actually. The game is a mix of a slice of life simulator (playing through almost every calendar date of an entire year), a visual novel where all you have to do is focus on the story, and classic jrpg action where you raid palaces in the metaverse, stylishly fighting enemies in turn based combat. As most of the game is story-driven, there's not too much to say about the gameplay apart from free time, and entering palaces/Mementos. One quip I had with free time was hanging out with confidants - the occasional extra filler hangout required to bond further with someone and get a new cut-scene felt largely unnecessary given the abundance of activities you could do elsewhere in the game. Apart from that, spending time with confidants was definitely a highlight of free time, with how real and developed most of the Persona cast feel.

The palaces in the game felt great. Kamoshida's castle admittedly gives the game a bit of a slow start with the introduction of the Metaverse, but the game only goes up from there. By the time you get to Madarame's flashy and golden museum, you really feel like as the player, you're on a HEIST and it's going down in style. The palaces following the theme of the seven deadly sins was a cute touch, especially considering that the game was all about stealing evil hearts. The ambience and atmosphere of the palaces also drastically differed (in a good way!), from cyber city outer space, pyramids, and a casino. The puzzles typically reflected the theme of the palace as well, keeping the raids feeling different and fun throughout the game. Combat felt moreorless like your typical jrpg, with default attacks, guarding, and special skills. The gun being a secondary option to a default swing made for some interesting management decisions in terms of palace raids and SP spent, and physical attack skills taking away your HP instead of SP was a fun mechanic to juggle with as well. Similar to how turn based combats tend to have "ultimate" abiltiies, P5R has "showtimes" and "all out attacks," featuring special cinematic attack animations. They're silly, cool, and leave you with a smile on your face. Balancing in the game felt just about right (I played on hard mode), and if I ever felt underleveled, I never had to grind for long to make up for it. Before I move on from palaces though - Okumura's boss fight was NOT it. The gimmicks were annoying, and felt punishing to the player for simply not being leveled up enough instead of encouraging strategy, given the time limit of wiping out mobs in one turn. Also, I wanted to square up with Okumura himself, not his goons. Grrrr. Every other boss fight gets a pass, though! Finally, the movement in the game felt a bit awkward at times. Like, you try to walk up to an npc to talk to them and overshoot a little, and have to re-adjust kind of awkward. It wasn't rough enough to take away from the gameplay, but making it a bit smoother would definitely make the game feel even better!

NARRATIVE: 5/5
For a game that's 100+ hours and largely story driven, I'm sure glad that Persona 5's story is TOP TIER. Woo! Honestly, all I have to say about this section is 'congrats to Persona 5 Royal for being the only video game to have Futaba Sakura.' Jokes aside, the character writing in this game is amazing. Some characters just feel so real and relatable, making any down time in the game to spend time with the cast a treat, instead of a chore. Even the less interesting characters like Ryuji, as forgettable as he is, is undeniably a bro. I found it so funny how Yusuke would claim he's not a pervert, and yet all the perverted dialogue options in his hangouts boosted your friendship the most. Futaba is undeniably best girl, and the game spoils you by including her in Sojiro's hangout storyline too (which is downright touching). I need to throw in that Goro Akechi is a hilarious character. No I will not be giving context. Just trust me on this one (source: dude trust me). Persona 5 manages to tackle a lot of serious and heartfelt issues in a wholesome and satisfactory way, instead of being overly clichéd and cringe. Having a likeable cast in a game like this is so important, and the end result is a game that feels like it's spoiling you for being as long as it is. Considering the sizeable number of confidants and party members as well, there's bound to be someone you like or connect with to some extent. The plot has a clear beginning and end, and has its fair shares of twists and turns. While some plot twists are all but expected (I won't be going into spoilers here), how exactly everything unfolds and plays out is usually where the story line delivers when it gets predictable. My favourite antagonist is easily the last one in the game (in the true ending). The complexity of the final villain in terms of their motivations and what their stance was on justice and the "greater good" felt refreshing and set apart from everyone else that came before them, and actually makes you want to pause and think for a moment if they really are the bad guy. Brilliant. I've heard before from people that have played P5R that they got depressed after beating the game, because it felt like they were leaving behind the friends that they made along the way. High praise that's honestly deserved, and speaks volumes of the world building and likeability of the character writing.

GRAPHICS: 5/5
It's one of those games that make you feel cool just for playing the game. The animation you get for ambushing an opponent? Getting behind them  on their shoulders, ripping off their mask? Kinda hot, if you ask me. HAHA. Character design and art are amazing, and the proof is that Futaba has glasses. The general aesthetic of the game is clean and pleasing, and a lot of touches to the art (including the white/black squares in the font) matches the theme of the Phantom Thieves. Plus points for creativity! The game always looks great to look at, minus that one enemy that looks like. Um. Anyways. P5R also adds animated anime-style story cutscenes, and they were all amazing as well! The game art design also pays attention to the personalities of the cast. One of my favourite examples is when the gang is sitting around together. Ryuji would be manspreading (LOL), Ann sitting up on the table, Makoto sitting like the prim and proper lady that she is, Yusuke standing around, Futaba lying down on her stomach... all these subtle touches to the art really shows how much care and thought has been put into this game, outside of the plot and gameplay.

SOUNDTRACK: 5/5
Chances are, you've heard Persona music before, even if you've never heard of or played the game series before. The music is iconic, catchy, and good. The music always gets the atmosphere juuust right, while being fun and engaging. About to re-enter someone's palace to steal their heart? You're about to feel real cool for it. Something sad is happening? Prepare for the music to make you depressed. The Persona soundtrack has surprisingly good diversity as well, flexibly allowing the music to enhance the game experience. What more could you ask for in a game soundtrack? As well, the voice acting for the entire cast is great, and suits the characters they represent. I can only imagine that the voice actor for Goro Akechi must've had a lot of fun ;)

OVERALL: 5/5
Persona 5 Royal is a phenomenal JRPG that sets a high standard for future games to come. Sure, the game is long, but considering how good the game is across the entirety of its length... it's a gift. You get over 100 hours of an immersive world with a diverse cast, in an emotional and cool rollercoaster of a game. If that doesn't sound fun to you, I recommend going on a merry-go-round instead. I'm sure you'll come around!

This game truly does feel life changing. It absorbs you until you finish it, and leaves you with a fresh new perspective on life. I started it early January, and only finished it early July. In this time it has become my favorite game, and I will be playing others in the series shortly. I hope you can get as much out of this game as I did :)

Much like the game's central theme of rehabilitation and rebellion, I was held prisoner of this story for the past five to six weeks, from which I finally broke free last night. 

I must be clear about something, I am a SMT veteran who never played a persona game before and I was not exactly thrilled by the social sim aspect of these games, so I walked in expecting absolutely nothing. despite that fact, I came through completely rehabilitated by this game. There's just.. something marvelous and undescribable about how this story presents itself and develops, even though all your characters follow your stereotypical tropes you still fall in love with and want to spend time with them, even in the most trivial and boring moments you actually have fun interacting with them. You actually spend so much time building your relationships with the cast that you want to see them succeed. The same can be said about most of the villains, most are well written and make themselves hated by the player through their exposition.

As an RPG fan I was looking forward to the dungeons and progression systems in this game, however they are rather simple, the combat is pretty much the same "exploit weakness to get extra turn" from the SMT series, which can be pretty cheeseable when you understand it. On the other hand, dungeons are few but well constructed, exactly what I expected from Atlus, nothing magnificent but mostly serviceable (aside from the spaceport, *uck that dungeon). There's also mementos, the "farm" dungeon where you go to grind levels and do sidequests, this was by far the weakest part of the game since the dungeon itself is procedurally generated, bland and ugly to look at. However it serves its purpose well.

The story starts pretty weird but quickly becomes incredible, when all pieces start coming into place and you can finally see the full picture the DLC campaing kicks in (you have to fulfill a very specific condition to even trigger this campaign, condition that was not exactly well telegraphed in-game), breaking the pace for a bit before wrapping the story up quite masterfully. 

This game goes beyond the recommendation, this is one of those games you have to experience for yourself, HOWEVER.. there's a catch. Persona 5R is rather lenghty, if you are a working adult with little time to play (like mysef) I think it'll be hard for you to enjoy the game properly, since the game is not only long, but demands lenghty play sessions to actually make some progress. Therefore, I can only recommend this game if you have a month or so to spare.


TL;DR: Wonderful game flipped my view on the social sim aspect, classic atlus experience gamewise, lovable characters, great story with some pacing issues towards the end. ACTUALLY CAN'T RECOMMEND THIS GAME TO WORKING ADULTS WITH LITTLE PLAYTIME.

Persona 5 Royal was my first Japanese RPG, and all I can say is: wow, wow, wow.

What impressed me most was the incredible depth of the game. At its core, Persona 5 Royal is about friendship and the connections you build with other people. If you don't enjoy reading dialogue, this probably isn't the game for you. But for me, all of that character development is exactly what made the experience so immersive. The relationships feel surprisingly fresh and most major characters are interesting in their own way.

I genuinely struggled to put this game down and ended up spending far more hours on it than I originally intended. The gameplay loop is incredibly addictive. Once you start playing, real-life time passes incredibly fast. The game encourages you to carefully manage your in-game days and take your time, but before you know it, you've spent hours completely immersed in its world.

For new players, my biggest recommendation is: don't look up too much online. There are spoilers everywhere, and the game is clearly designed to be explored at your own pace. The freedom to make your own choices is a huge part of its charm. You don't need to min-max everything to finish the game, although it's possible to miss some bonus content if you make certain decisions along the way.

Another thing that deserves special praise is the soundtrack. It's absolutely fantastic. I downloaded it after finishing the game and still listen to it regularly.

A fair warning: this is a very long game and that won't appeal to everyone. The story was surprisingly good, written from the perspective of teenagers while still being engaging and relatable for adults like myself. And when it all comes together, the payoff feels earned. After spending so much time with these characters and sharing so many experiences with them, saying goodbye is genuinely bittersweet.

Persona 5 is a really fantastic Japanese RPG.  Originally releasing 10 years ago, this game has directly influenced a lot of more recent RPG's that you may have played.  Claire Obscure: Expedition 33 being one of the very direct ones.  This Royal edition adds the DLC for P5, notably an extra semester and new characters.  The game is extremely stylish and explores sociology well.  This review is after rolling credits and getting 100% on the achievement list, which took me 134 hours.

[h2] What makes Persona unique? [/h2]
So the last Persona game I played was Persona 2: Eternal Punishment back when it was new on the PS1.  There's a few things that standout to me as hardcoded in the Persona game DNA:
[b] The real focus of the game is on saving individual people. [/b]  In this game, really each major mission is about changing someone's mind.  
[b] You can talk with your enemies in combat. [/b]  You can recruit them like in Pokemon or shake them down for money or items.  Interestingly the first Persona and the first Pokemon came out in the same year.  The enemies have opinions and moods, they are living their life too.

This is a game that unironically wants you to feel like you live in a society.  

Since I skipped 3 and 4 and went straight to 5 there a few things that have changed that jumped out at me from the start.  The story is less "casually dark".  If you don't know what an invoker is don't look it up.  Dark stuff happens, but when it does it is given weight.  And the dungeons are less "Wizardry" and more "Earthbound".  Instead of bumping around corridors in first person, you are in third person and can see the encounters walking around.  

The social link system is something that was added sometime after 2 as well.  Each person that is in your social circle is given a Tarot that can be leveled up.  Leveling up that relationship gives you abilities like "Make Curry" or "Grow Plants" or in combat things like "Change Party Members" or "Chance to Remove Status Effects".  And story beats, each person has their own thing going on.  Those story beats are really the heart of the game.

[h2] What is playing the game like? [/h2]
Combat is more fun the more attention you pay to it.  Enemies often have a weakness to a specific damage type.  If you hit them with that weakness, they fall down and you get to "Pass the Baton" to one of your other party members.  That boosts that characters' stats and lets them take their turn now as well as later.  You can do this 4 times per move, but you can only knock down each enemy once.  So combat is super exploitable.  If you knock down the whole team then your entire team gets a large, very effective attack on the whole other team.  The game can turn into a puzzle to figure out how to win on turn 1 so that they don't get a turn, which keeps it interesting.  

So that said, I found the actual combat to be pretty easy.  I expected that going in and set the difficulty to Hard at the start and never changed it.  As best I can tell, "Hard" means that you'll just sometimes get one-shot.  It didn't do it so much that it felt cheesy to me.  I started on Hard based on my experience in the first 2 games.  I was expecting for combat items and status effects to be crazy good when used correctly, and I was right.

It is worth calling out too, there are no real-time elements that I remember in the combat.  No dodge/parry or other things needed.

The rest of the game is time management, which is better than it sounds like.  The base game is April - December and the expansion is January - February.  You will play each day as a Japanese teenager, so you are going to school and you (the player) will take part of their exams.  Most days you will have an afternoon time slot and an evening time slot.  At those times you'll need to go meet with individual people in your social circle, work a job, shoot pool or play darts, do your laundry, or explore dungeons.  I am probably not selling this part very well, but it really is the best part of the game.

The Pokemon aspects are a little different than in other games like that.  Instead of growing one and getting attached to it, you need to cycle through those constantly.  That system is really deep for those of you who want to explore it, which is optional.

Did I mention the music is fantastic?  Because it is.

[h2] Take your time [/h2]
It is worth calling out specifically that this is a long game.  It needs that room to work.  If you try to rush it, I doubt you will have a good time.  So go into it knowing that.

Which brings me to criticisms:
[b] Its starting to feel a little dated [/b]  There are a lot of games that have been influenced by this game since it came out and they have made some improvements.  E33 as mentioned above is a good example of that.  Make no mistake, this is a 10 year old game now.
[b] Sometimes you get stuck in a long section of talking [/b]  Sometimes the game decides for you that you need to do a certain thing on a day, or that you can't go out tonight.  This is not a 'Save Anywhere' game so you may end up stuck in a long section when you are needing to stop playing for a while.
[b] The menus are stylish but can be annoying to navigate [/b]  And they use a lot of Japanese words.  There were times where I was looking for the item that did 50 Psi damage or Bless damage and I would have to go through every item's description to find them.  Those are Psy Magatama and the Happy Bomb btw.
[b] You will probably want to use a wiki to navigate the persona upgrade system [/b]  And there is a fantastic one out there.  The system is complex and deep.
[b] You can accidentally miss the 3rd semester DLC [/b]  The game does not make that clear.  It is easy to get into it though, just make sure you spend a lot of time with your school's guidance councilor.  Otherwise the game is pretty easy to 100% in one playthrough.

[h2] So wrapping this up [/h2]
This is one of the most "Japanese" JRPG's out there.  It does a really good job of telling a lot of smaller-scale personal stories.  You'll get attached to each of the 23 confidants.  I feel like I could go on, but instead I'll just express that after finishing the game I am sitting here trying to figure out what I should do now.  Typically I am ready to move on to a different game when finishing one, especially after longer games like this.  I have not really felt like this since finishing Elden Ring, which I think is the biggest compliment that I can give.
